title: How do we write a number without landmark symbols?
description: Three thousand seven hundred twenty five is grouped into landmarks, and then the landmark symbols are dropped so that only the position tells which landmark. Keeko's doubt is that the digits can be cut in pairs.
teaching_notes: One idea: group the number by the landmarks first, then write only the counts, with each place standing for one landmark. Watch for students who cut the digits of the number into pairs instead of grouping by landmarks.

source: Write 3725 in the Mesopotamian place value system, using our numerals for each place.
video_script.why: The child groups a number by the landmarks one, sixty and three thousand six hundred, then drops the landmark symbols so that the place of each count shows its landmark.
video_script.substitution: Group the number by landmarks first, then write only the counts in the order of the landmarks.
video_script.anchor: the book's Mesopotamian places: ones on the right, sixties next, then three thousand six hundreds
video_script.wrong_answer: thirty seven in the sixties place and twenty five in the ones place
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko cuts 3725 into 37 and 25 and writes 37 | 25; but 37 x 60 + 25 = 2245, not 3725, because the places must follow the landmarks
video_script.payoff_line: Three thousand seven hundred twenty five is written one, then two, then five.

final_answer.spoken: one, then two, then five, from one lot of three thousand six hundred, two sixties and five

maths_rules: dropping the landmark symbols: 1 in the 3600s place, 2 in the 60s place, 5 in the 1s place, written 1 | 2 | 5
Keeko's slip: 37 | 25 means 37 x 60 + 25 = 2220 + 25 = 2245, which is 1480 too small
video_script.design: One idea: the place of a count shows its landmark. Three columns labelled 3600, 60 and 1 stay on the board while the counts drop into them.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; three empty places in a row; the number 3725 beside them

marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.places: three empty places appear in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the Mesopotamian way of writing numbers.
<bookmark mark='places'/>Each place in a row holds one count, written with our own numerals.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We must write three thousand seven hundred twenty five in these places. What will each place show?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board with the empty places

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the landmark symbols fade away; three columns remain, labelled 3600, 60 and 1 from the left; the words place value system appear under them

marks.cols: three columns remain labelled 3600, 60 and 1 from the left
marks.name: the words place value system appear under the columns

narration: <bookmark mark='drop'/>The Mesopotamians dropped the landmark symbols altogether. The rightmost place counts the ones, and the next place counts the sixties.
<bookmark mark='cols'/>The place after that counts the three thousand six hundreds.
<bookmark mark='name'/>When the position of a count tells its landmark, we call it a place value system.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the number three thousand seven hundred twenty five.

beats.on_screen: To find: the count in each place

marks.find: the words the count in each place are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the count that goes in each place.
<bookmark mark='fit'/>Step one, see how many three thousand six hundreds fit. One fits.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Three thousand seven hundred twenty five take away three thousand six hundred leaves one hundred twenty five.

marks.two: two 60s are taken out of 125 and 2 x 60 = 120 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, see how many sixties fit in one hundred twenty five. Two sixties make one hundred twenty.
<bookmark mark='five'/>One hundred twenty five take away one hundred twenty leaves five ones.

beats.on_screen: 3725 as one 3600, two 60s and five 1s; check: 3600 + 120 + 5 = 3725

marks.group: the grouping of one 3600, two 60s and five 1s is written

narration: <bookmark mark='group'/>Step three, put the groups together. We have one three thousand six hundred, two sixties and five ones.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check by adding. Three thousand six hundred, one hundred twenty and five make three thousand seven hundred twenty five.

beats.on_screen: counts dropped into places: 3600s place gets 1, 60s place gets 2, 1s place gets 5

marks.drop: the counts 1, 2 and 5 drop into the three places
marks.read: each place is read with its landmark

narration: <bookmark mark='drop'/>Step four, drop the landmark symbols and keep only the counts. Each count goes into the place of its landmark.
<bookmark mark='read'/>The big place gets one, the sixties place gets two, and the ones place gets five.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Three thousand seven hundred twenty five is written one, then two, then five.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the three places
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's two places holding 37 and 25 with the label 37 x 60 + 25 = 2245; 2245 shown short of 3725; the places are replaced by 1, 2 and 5

marks.fix: the places are replaced by 1, 2 and 5

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko cuts the digits in pairs. Keeko says it is thirty seven in the sixties place and twenty five in the ones place.
<bookmark mark='read'/>That would be thirty seven sixties and twenty five, which is only two thousand two hundred forty five.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Cutting the digits does not follow the landmarks. We must group by three thousand six hundreds, sixties and ones first.
